summary: This standards-track RFC provides the External Data Representation (XDR) description of NFS version 4 minor version 2, the machine-readable definition of its data structures.

eli5.summary: The exact blueprint of the messages NFS 4.2 sends, written in a language programs can read.

questions: how to extract the nfs xdr file from the rfc
what are the new operations in nfs 4.2
subtitle: The machine-readable blueprint of every message, constant and error code in NFS version 4.2.

tldr.problem: Implementers of NFS version 4.2 need an exact, compilable description of the data structures that go on the wire, separate from the prose protocol document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC contains the complete XDR description of NFSv4.2, with a small shell script that extracts it from the document into a file ready to compile.
tldr.outcome: It is the formal companion to the NFSv4.2 protocol specification in RFC 7862 and reconverges the XDR of NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1.

today: RFC 7863 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the XDR companion to RFC 7862.

sections.title: What This Document Contains
sections.content:
RFC 7863 holds the External Data Representation (XDR) description of the NFSv4.2 protocol. XDR is the notation defined in RFC 4506 for describing data that goes on the wire. The protocol itself, with its behavior and rules, is specified in RFC 7862; this document is the formal description of the data structures that protocol uses.

The document is almost entirely code. The only prose covers how to use the code, a security pointer and an IANA pointer. The key words MUST, SHOULD and so on are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: One book explains how NFS 4.2 behaves. This one is just the exact shapes of the messages, like the cutting guide for a sewing pattern.

sections.title: Covering NFSv4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 Together
sections.content:
To help implementations that support all of NFSv4.0, NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.2, the description includes operations and features of NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 that do not apply to NFSv4.2. It is fully compatible with the NFSv4.0 specification in RFC 7531, with one exception.

The exception is the clientaddr4 structure. It has been replaced by (strictly, aliased to) netaddr4, which has the same members with the same purposes under new names: r_netid becomes na_r_netid and r_addr becomes na_r_addr. The RFC says this effectively fully reconverges the NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 (RFC 5662) strands of the XDR.
sections.eli5: There used to be two slightly different copies of the plans, one for each older version. This RFC glues them back into one plan, with one part renamed so both match.

sections.title: Extracting the Machine-Readable File
sections.content:
Every line of XDR in the document starts with the sentinel ///. A two-stage shell script keeps only the lines with that sentinel and strips the leading white space and the sentinel itself. If the script is saved as extract.sh and the RFC text as spec.txt, running sh extract.sh < spec.txt > nfs4_prot.x produces the file that can be compiled.

The output starts with a license header and then some pass-through lines (those beginning with %) that pull in the auth_sys definitions for the C code generated later.
sections.eli5: Every line you need is marked with a little flag. A tiny program picks out the flagged lines and gives you a clean file a computer can use.

sections.title: Constants, Types and File Attributes
sections.content:
The first part defines sizes and basic types. Examples are NFS4_FHSIZE (128), NFS4_VERIFIER_SIZE (8), NFS4_OTHER_SIZE (12), NFS4_OPAQUE_LIMIT (1024) and NFS4_SESSIONID_SIZE (16). File handles, verifiers, session IDs, UTF-8 strings and pathnames all get their own typedefs.

It then defines the file types in nfs_ftype4 (regular file, directory, block and character devices, symbolic link, socket, fifo, attribute directory and named attribute), the time structure nfstime4, file system IDs, file system location structures, and the many constants for access control entries: ACE types, flags and masks.
sections.eli5: This part is the list of measuring cups and building blocks: how long a file's ID can be, what kinds of files exist, and how to write down a time.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
The nfsstat4 enumeration lists every status a server can return, starting with NFS4_OK = 0. The numbers follow history: the early NFSv3-style codes are small (for example NFS4ERR_NOENT = 2 and NFS4ERR_ACCESS = 13), and the NFSv4 codes begin at 10001 (NFS4ERR_BADHANDLE).

The list is split into blocks by version: a comment marks where NFSv4.1 errors start (from 10049) and where NFSv4.2 errors start. The NFSv4.2 additions are 10088 to 10094, such as NFS4ERR_OFFLOAD_DENIED and NFS4ERR_BADLABEL. Value 19 is deliberately never allocated because it was used in NFSv3 and a value must not mean something different in NFSv4.x. A comment also notes NFS4ERR_RESOURCE is not a valid error in NFSv4.1.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the server answers with a number that means a reason, like a list of reasons a teacher might write on your homework. Number 19 is skipped on purpose to avoid confusion with an older list.

sections.title: Operations and the COMPOUND Message
sections.content:
The enumeration nfs_opnum4 gives each operation a number, and two unions (nfs_argop4 for requests, nfs_resop4 for results) pick the right argument or result structure for each one. A request, COMPOUND4args, carries a tag, a minorversion and an array of operations. The reply, COMPOUND4res, has a status, the tag and an array of results.

The RPC program definition is short. NFS4_PROGRAM is program 100003, version 4, with just two procedures: NFSPROC4_NULL (0) and NFSPROC4_COMPOUND (1). Callbacks from server to client use NFS4_CALLBACK, program number 0x40000000 in the transient range, version 1, with CB_NULL (0) and CB_COMPOUND (1). The client assigns the exact transient number and gives it to the server through CREATE_SESSION or BACKCHANNEL_CTL. An OP_ILLEGAL value of 10044 is also defined.
sections.eli5: Instead of many tiny letters, the client puts a whole list of requests in one envelope called COMPOUND, and the server replies with one envelope of answers.

sections.title: Operations New in NFSv4.2
sections.content: The operation numbers 59 to 71 are the NFSv4.2 additions: ALLOCATE, COPY, COPY_NOTIFY, DEALLOCATE, IO_ADVISE, LAYOUTERROR, LAYOUTSTATS, OFFLOAD_CANCEL, OFFLOAD_STATUS, READ_PLUS, SEEK, WRITE_SAME and CLONE. Each appears in the request and result unions with its own argument and result structures. What these operations mean and how they behave is defined in RFC 7862, not here.
sections.eli5: NFS 4.2 added thirteen new things you can ask a server to do. This RFC only gives the shape of each request; the other RFC explains what each one does.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is one line: see the Security Considerations section of RFC 7862. The IANA Considerations section likewise points to RFC 7862.
sections.eli5: The safety rules and the registry notes are kept in the main NFS 4.2 book, so this one just points you there.
